docs.title: gerrymander
docs.text: A hostname and port control plane. One authority for who owns which hostname in a wildcard zone, and which process owns which port on a dev machine. The same binary, model, and CLI run on a laptop and in production.

docs.title: Sixty seconds to a real hostname
docs.text:
curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Nano112/gerrymander/main/install.sh | sh

The installer detects your platform, installs the binary, puts the daemon on login, wires DNS for dev zones, and installs the TLS trust. Everything it writes is reversible and marker-tagged. If you prefer brew, brew install nano112/tap/gerry && gerry bootstrap does the same. Then:

cd my-app && gerry init            # scaffolds gerrymander.yaml
bun run dev                        # → https://my-app.test, trusted TLS, done

gerry uninstall removes exactly what setup created and can never break DNS it didn't set up.

docs.title: What it solves
docs.text:
Multi-tenant SaaS on *.yourdomain.com has an implicit race: the app's tenant table and the platform's ingress both think they own the hostname namespace, and neither can see the other. Nothing stops a tenant claiming grafana; nothing stops an engineer shadowing tenant acme with a new route. Meanwhile on every dev machine, 5173 and 8000 are allocated by convention and collide weekly.

Both are the same operation: claim a scarce name from a pool, exclusively, and make traffic arrive. gerrymander is that operation as a service.

  • Registry: UNIQUE(zone, label) over tenant claims, platform reservations, and a reserved-word blocklist, in one namespace. Sticky port pools with the same semantics.
  • Dev mode: TLS proxy with its own CA, embedded DNS, process supervision, docker relays, a Vite plugin, and compose-label auto-claim. bun run dev is the whole interface.
  • Kubernetes: an observer that audits what your ingress actually serves against the registry (with Prometheus alerts), and an actuator that materializes routes (Traefik or Gateway API) from allocations. It only ever touches resources it labeled itself, and a CI e2e proves that on every change.
  • Scoped tokens: hand a tenant or CI job a credential that can manage its own hostnames and nothing else.
  • MCP: your AI agent asks the registry for a port and a hostname instead of guessing 8000. See AI agents.

docs.title: Where next
docs.text:
• Quickstart: local dev, end to end
  • Frameworks: Vite, Python, docker, anything
  • Kubernetes: observer, actuator, Helm, GitOps CRD
  • Scoped tokens: multi-tenant credentials and the audit trail

docs.title: AI agents (MCP)
docs.text: Every coding agent eventually starts a dev server, and every one of them guesses port 8000, into a port that's already taken, on a machine it can't see. gerrymander ships an MCP server so agents allocate instead of guessing.

docs.title: Register
docs.text:
claude mcp add gerry -- gerry mcp

(Any MCP-capable client works; gerry mcp speaks MCP over stdio and talks to the local daemon.)

docs.title: What the agent gets
docs.text:
• ports: claim a sticky port for a named owner. The same owner gets the same port next session, from a pool that avoids the crowded defaults.
  • hostnames: check availability, claim api.myproject.test, list and release, so an agent can set up a working https:// dev URL end to end, including for a container it just started.
  • status: what's registered, what's listening, what the proxy routes. The machine's actual state instead of the agent's assumptions.

docs.title: The skill (Claude Code)
docs.text:
The repo ships an agent skill that teaches the rules — allocate instead of guess, read gerry status before killing listeners, release what you create:

mkdir -p ~/.claude/skills && cp -r skills/gerry ~/.claude/skills/gerry

Project-local installs work the same way into .claude/skills/.

docs.title: Why this beats "just pick a port"
docs.text:
The failure mode isn't picking a port. It's two agents (or an agent and you) picking the same one, or an agent leaving stale processes on ports it forgot. Registry semantics fix both: claims are exclusive and owned, so a second claim by the same owner returns the same port (idempotent), a different owner gets a different one, and gerry ls / the desktop app show exactly who holds what, with supervised processes stoppable by name.

Give a long-running agent a scoped token and it can manage its own project's hostnames without being able to touch anything else.

docs.title: Application and service catalog
docs.text: Gerry's catalog is the shared identity library for developer tools, infrastructure views and application launchers. It works in the same local SQLite daemon as hostname allocation; it needs no AWS account or cloud registry. A deployed Gerry instance exposes the same API with authenticated readers.

docs.title: Contract
docs.text:
Entity Purpose Identity Application Project name, description, logo, icon, color and links Stable id; editable display name Service An application component and its role Stable id and manifest key Deployment One service in an environment and optional workspace Stable id, explicit environment, workspace and zone Resource A declared database, bucket, server or other dependency Stable id, kind, provider/native id, related service ids Capabilities Permission labels, entry permission and role definitions Immutable (service_id, version) Asset A logo available independently of the source checkout Immutable SHA-256 digest

The public Go package github.com/Nano112/gerrymander/catalog contains the typed schema and client. JSON responses declare schema_version: 1. Routes and ports remain separate existing APIs. The catalog never extracts supervised commands, environment variables, credentials, user grants or tenant allocations.

Resources are declared inventory, not discovered or verified infrastructure. An AWS ARN or other provider id can correlate a declaration with future discovery. Neither registered nor inactive is a health measurement. Monitoring systems continue to own observations, alerts, packet data and time-series metrics.

docs.title: Declare and publish
docs.text:
See the runnable example. Existing routing manifests need no new fields: applying them also registers their app, services and development deployments. Explicit ids are recommended before external consumers start storing references. Keep them unchanged when renaming display labels.

project: atlas
application:
  id: app:atlas
  display:
    name: Atlas
    logo: ./logo.svg
    icon: application
    color: '#7259DB'
    links:
      docs: https://example.com/docs
environment: development
workspace: alice
zone: atlas-alice.test
services:
  web:
    id: atlas-web
    role: web
    display:
      name: Atlas console
    hostnames: [atlas-alice.test]
    port_pool: dev
    capabilities:
      version: v1
      entry_permission: access
      permissions:
        access: Open console
        jobs.read: Read jobs
      roles:
        viewer: [access, jobs.read]
    deployment:
      capability_version: v1
resources:
  database:
    kind: database
    provider: local
    display:
      name: Development database
      icon: postgres
    services: [web]

gerry up -f examples/catalog/gerrymander.yaml
gerry catalog --application app:atlas
gerry catalog --access --environment development --workspace alice
gerry down -f examples/catalog/gerrymander.yaml

gerry up, gerry dev and the updated Vite plugin import relative logo files before applying the manifest. Files must stay inside the manifest directory, including symlink targets. PNG, JPEG and static SVG are supported up to 512 KiB; SVG scripts, CSS, embedded documents and external references are rejected. API publishers upload an asset first and use its sha256:… reference; the daemon never reads a client-provided file path. Direct API users must send prepared YAML.

For an existing remotely hosted application use catalog_only: true on the service and deployment.launch_url: https://example.com. Such a service declares no routing backend, hostname or dev command. Catalog-only/resource-only manifests need no zone and do not create or prune routes.

Default ids derive from project/service keys and deployment scope. Supplying application.id, service id, deployment.id or resource id overrides those defaults. Existing service-access keys can be retained as service ids. Service keys, parent identities and deployment environment/workspace/zone/owner are immutable; use a new deployment id when moving between scopes. Display data and deployment endpoints can change. Service display fields inherit from their application in access responses; generic consumers can call InheritDisplay.

docs.title: Local workspaces and lifecycle
docs.text:
The default environment is development; set production explicitly in a production manifest. Workspace is optional and defaults to an empty shared workspace. Consumers must select both environment and workspace, rather than guessing from hostnames. A read token can inspect the whole registry: these selectors are filtering, not tenant authorization boundaries.

Without a workspace, legacy routing ownership remains project/service. Opting into a workspace uses project@workspace/service and separate sticky ports. Use distinct dev zones/hostnames for different workspaces: declaring a workspace does not let it take another workspace's hostname. Use separate local and production daemons; changing an environment label is not a routing sandbox.

gerry up retains its additive routing behavior; --prune releases routes and deactivates deployments removed from that manifest scope. gerry dev and the Vite plugin prune by default. gerry down releases declared routes and marks the declared deployments inactive. Identities, version history and declared resources are retained. Omission from a bundle does not delete them. Resource deletion, provider reconciliation and garbage collection are not yet implemented.

Catalog bundle writes are transactional. Manifest apply preflights catalog conflicts before route changes, then publishes after routing succeeds. Routing and catalog publication are separate transactions; an interrupted or conflicting apply can require a retry. This follows existing route reconciliation semantics.

docs.title: Service Access integration
docs.text:
Gerry publishes definitions, not authorization decisions. An access system continues to own accounts, membership, grants, API credentials, expiry and audit. Store grants against stable service ids and permission keys, never display names.

  1. Publish a capability version in capabilities.
  2. Explicitly select it with deployment.capability_version.
  3. Read the access catalog for the intended environment/workspace.

Publishing v2 never activates it. A different definition under an existing version returns HTTP 409. The access endpoint includes only registered deployments with an explicitly selected, published version; it never selects "latest". Omitting the selection removes that deployment from access discovery on its next apply. Review version changes before activating them. Preserve explicit permission grants during that migration rather than automatically expanding named roles.

On a catalog outage, consumers should retain a known, reviewed definition snapshot and fail closed for unknown service ids or permissions. Do not replace the permission universe with an empty allowlist or grant access because discovery is unavailable. Existing uptime probes can continue from their last inventory.

docs.title: API and libraries
docs.text:
Mint a server-side reader with gerry token create service-catalog --scope catalog-read. This scope can read every catalog identity, version and asset, but cannot access allocation/port APIs or change routes, manifests, metadata or credentials. Owner tokens cannot read the catalog. Admin/root credentials publish it.

Method Endpoint Result GET /v1/catalog?application_id=app:atlas Full snapshot; app filter optional GET /v1/catalog/access?environment=production&workspace= {schema_version, services: AccessEntry[]} POST /v1/catalog/apply Publish one typed Bundle POST /v1/catalog/assets Upload {data: base64}; returns {id, media_type} GET /v1/catalog/assets/{id} Authenticated image bytes, ETag and restrictive CSP POST /v1/catalog/deployments/{id}/deactivate Retire deployment from discovery

The Go client exposes Snapshot, Access, Apply, UploadAsset and Deactivate. The Laravel client exposes catalog(), accessCatalog($environment, $workspace) and catalogAsset($id). Use backend credentials and proxy image bytes through the consumer's authenticated origin; do not expose registry tokens in browser URLs. Multiple registered deployments of a service can appear in the same scope; consumers must group by service id or choose a deployment explicitly.

The infra portal and Olsyn Service Access can now adopt this contract. This update does not migrate their existing configuration or switch their authorization. Desktop routing views continue to use allocations; catalog metadata is available to local tools through the CLI and the same API.

docs.title: Upgrade and verification
docs.text:
Deploy the updated daemon before updated clients. SQLite/PostgreSQL migrations add catalog tables without modifying allocation, port or token records. The catalog is backed by the same database; include it in normal Gerry backups.

The root CI runs go vet ./... and go test -race ./.... Vite logo-import tests run with npm ci && npm test in clients/vite. Optional PostgreSQL catalog tests use GERRY_TEST_POSTGRES_DSN=... go test -race ./internal/store -run TestCatalog; they create and remove isolated schemas in the specified test database. CI also runs those tests against PostgreSQL 16 and exercises the Laravel SDK with composer install && php tests/catalog.php in clients/laravel.

docs.title: Uptime check definitions
docs.text:
Deployments can declare optional checks with a stable id, name, HTTP(S) url, description, accepted statuses (default 200), contains, scalar json expectations, and a redirect expectation (origin and YAML path_prefix; JSON pathPrefix). Consumers choose which environments and networks to probe. No check is inferred from a hostname or tenant allocation, and Gerry never runs checks. Probe credentials remain with the monitoring consumer. Check ids must be unique within each application bundle; consumers also reject collisions across applications. Independent monitors should persist a last-known-good snapshot and continue checks if the catalog is unavailable, while displaying discovery age.

Container builds publish immutable ghcr.io/nano112/gerrymander:sha-<commit> tags for amd64 and arm64 after tests pass. Production deployments should pin a reviewed image digest. This workflow does not change running clusters.

Scheduled inventory publishers can use catalog-write tokens. They can read and publish catalog metadata/assets and retire deployments, but cannot change routing, ports, zones, processes or credentials. Like catalog-read, the scope is registry-wide; it is not a per-application authorization boundary.

docs.title: Coexistence: what gerry touches, what it never touches
docs.text: gerry's rule for living on your machine: every takeover is detected before it happens, and every removal requires gerry's own ownership mark. gerry uninstall is dry-run by default and can list its entire footprint.

docs.title: The footprint (complete inventory)
docs.text:
Thing Created by Marked how Removed by uninstall? launchd plist / systemd user unit gerry service install fixed name (com.gerrymander.daemon / gerrymander.service) yes /etc/resolver/<tld> (macOS) gerry setup first line # gerrymander-managed only with the marker System-trust CA gerry trust CN gerrymander local CA only that CN docker relay containers docker backends label app.gerrymander.relay yes (by label) ~/.gerrymander/ (db, CA, config, logs) daemon path only with --purge the gerry binary you — never (told where it is)

Why uninstall cannot break DNS: the only DNS artifact gerry ever creates is a marker-tagged per-TLD resolver file. Removing it restores the exact pre-gerry path: your upstream resolver answers, and dev TLDs simply NXDOMAIN. Resolver files without the marker (dnsmasq's, Herd's, yours) are reported and left alone, always. Same logic for TLS: a CA gerry merely borrowed (say, Caddy's already-trusted root) has a different CN and is never deleted.

docs.title: Interference matrix, and what gerry does about each
docs.text:
Ports 80/443 taken (Herd, Valet, Caddy, nginx, another proxy, a docker container): the proxy degrades instead of dying. The registry API stays up, the log and gerry status name the process holding the port (via lsof) with the choice: stop it or move proxy.tls in the config.

Port 4780 taken: if the holder answers like a gerry daemon, the error says so explicitly ("container mode running? stop it first"); the two-daemons foot-gun is caught at startup, not debugged at midnight.

Existing dev-DNS (dnsmasq, Herd, Valet): gerry setup probes resolution first and skips any TLD that already resolves, naming the likely owner. gerry never edits another tool's files.

systemd-resolved / VPN DNS (Tailscale MagicDNS etc.): macOS per-TLD resolver files coexist with VPN DNS. On Linux gerry prints manual routing instructions rather than guessing at resolved's config.

Intercepting proxies (Proxyman, Charles, corporate): gerry status detects an active system/env HTTP proxy and warns. The signature is "works in curl, dies in the browser", and the stale-socket variant survives daemon restarts (learned the hard way).

mDNSResponder on 5353: gerry's embedded DNS binds unicast 127.0.0.1:5353, which coexists with mDNS multicast; resolver files carry an explicit port 5353 line.

OS ephemeral port range (macOS hands out 49152–65535): sticky grants are bind-tested before issue and marked occupied-foreign when something unmanaged squats later: reported, never silently reassigned.

Preloaded-HSTS TLDs: .dev, .app and friends are real, HSTS-preloaded gTLDs; browsers refuse local CAs for them. Use .test (RFC 6761 reserved).

Firefox: keeps its own trust store; import the CA there manually or enable security.enterprise_roots.enabled.

Docker absent/stopped: docker backends fail with a clear error and everything else keeps working; relays restart themselves (--restart unless-stopped) when docker returns.

docs.title: Framework recipes
docs.text:
gerry integrates through two primitives, a routed hostname and a sticky port, so "integration" is mostly which of two mechanisms hands your tool its port:

Mechanism For How gerrymander-vite plugin Anything vite-based One plugin line; applies the manifest, sets port/allowedHosts/origin/HMR itself gerry run Everything else gerry run --owner proj/svc -- CMD --port '{PORT}': sets $PORT, substitutes {PORT}, execs

Verification status is labeled honestly: ✅ ran here end-to-end, 🔶 same primitives, not yet exercised.

docs.title: ✅ Vite (React, Vue, plain): plugin
docs.text:
// vite.config.ts
import gerrymander from "gerrymander-vite";
export default defineConfig({ plugins: [react(), gerrymander()] });
bun run dev / npm run dev is the whole workflow. Verified end-to-end in examples/coolwebsite (bun runtime, HMR over wss, rename-and-prune).

docs.title: ✅ Python (FastAPI / Django / Flask): gerry dev
docs.text:
Declare the command in the manifest and the whole workflow is one word:

services:
  api:
    hostnames: [api.myproj.test]
    port_pool: dev
    dev: uv run uvicorn main:app --port {PORT} --reload

gerry dev api    # applies the manifest, grants the sticky port, runs it
gerry run --owner myproj/api -- CMD --port '{PORT}' remains the ad-hoc form. Remember CORS when the frontend lives on a sibling hostname; see the example's backend/main.py.

docs.title: ✅ Dockerized apps: docker backend (auto-relay)
docs.text:
A container that publishes no ports can still be a backend: gerry keeps a tiny socat relay on its network, publishing a sticky loopback port on demand. Zero compose edits.

services:
  app:
    hostnames: [myproj.test, "*.myproj.test"]
    docker: { network: myproj_default, host: laravel.test, port: 80 }
Verified live: an unpublished nginx:alpine served over TLS through the proxy, relay auto-created on first request (docker ps shows it as gerry-relay-*, labeled app.gerrymander.relay). Needs the docker CLI on the daemon's host; first use pulls alpine/socat.

docs.title: ✅ Laravel Sail: docker backend + one manifest
docs.text:
Sail is the docker-backend case with two wrinkles: the app and its Vite dev server live in the same container on different ports, and the app itself wants to talk back to the registry.

Give the container a stable network alias, then route both ports at it:

# docker-compose.yml
services:
  laravel.test:
    networks:
      sail:
      dev-proxy:            # external: true
        aliases: [myapp]

# gerrymander.yaml
project: myapp
zone: myapp.test
services:
  app:
    hostnames: [myapp.test, "*.myapp.test"]   # wildcard = tenant subdomains
    routes:
      - docker: { network: dev-proxy, host: myapp, port: 80 }
      - listen: 5175
        docker: { network: dev-proxy, host: myapp, port: 5175 }
    dev: ./scripts/dev-stack.sh

Vite over TLS without certs in the container. Add the Vite port to proxy.extra_tls_ports and gerry terminates TLS on it, so Vite serves plain http and still loads as https:// assets with working wss:// HMR from every tenant subdomain:

# ~/.gerrymander/gerry.yaml
proxy:
  extra_tls_ports: [5173, 5174, 5175, 5176]

// vite.config.js — no https block; gerry owns TLS
server: {
  host: '0.0.0.0', port: 5175, strictPort: true, cors: true,
  origin: 'https://myapp.test:5175',
  hmr: { host: 'myapp.test', clientPort: 5175, protocol: 'wss' },
}

Letting the app reach the registry. A container cannot reach a registry bound to 127.0.0.1, and widening api.listen to 0.0.0.0 publishes it to the LAN. @docker binds the docker bridge gateways instead — exactly the address containers already know as host.docker.internal, and nothing that routes off-host:

# ~/.gerrymander/gerry.yaml
api:
  listen: 127.0.0.1:4780
  extra_listen: ["@docker"]

# .env
GERRY_API=http://host.docker.internal:4780
GERRY_ZONE=myapp.test

Now composer require gerrymander/laravel gives the app availability checks (Gerrymander\Rules\HostnameAvailable), a backfill command (artisan hostname:sync), and — for stancl/tenancy — a listener that claims and releases hostnames as domains are created and deleted. With GERRY_API unset the whole package goes inert, so CI needs no daemon. See clients/laravel.

gerry status checks this path end to end: whether the docker daemon answers this user, whether the manifest's network exists, and whether each alias resolves on it — the three failures that all look like a 502.

docs.title: ✅ Bun runtime: either
docs.text:
bunx --bun vite works under the plugin (verified). A native server:

// Bun.serve reads $PORT by convention; gerry run provides it.
Bun.serve({ port: Number(process.env.PORT), fetch: handler });

gerry run --owner myproj/api -- bun run server.ts

docs.title: 🔶 SvelteKit / Astro / Nuxt: plugin (vite-based)
docs.text:
All three embed vite, so gerrymander-vite slots into their vite plugin arrays:

// svelte.config.js consumers: vite.config.ts as usual
export default defineConfig({ plugins: [sveltekit(), gerrymander()] });
// astro.config.mjs
export default defineConfig({ vite: { plugins: [gerrymander()] } });
Caveat to watch: each framework layers its own server defaults; if one overrides the port after plugins run, fall back to gerry run + framework port flag.

docs.title: 🔶 Next.js: gerry run
docs.text:
Next isn't vite; the courier does it:

gerry run --owner myproj/web -- next dev -p '{PORT}'
Next 15+ blocks cross-origin dev assets like Vite does. Add your hostname:

// next.config.js
module.exports = { allowedDevOrigins: ["myproj.test"] };
HMR: Next's websocket uses the page origin, so it flows through the proxy without extra config.

docs.title: 🔶 Rails / Django / Go / anything
docs.text:
gerry run --owner myproj/app -- rails server -p '{PORT}'
gerry run --owner myproj/app -- python manage.py runserver '127.0.0.1:{PORT}'
gerry run --owner myproj/app -- go run . --addr ':{PORT}'

docs.title: The manifest that backs all of these
docs.text:
project: myproj
zone: myproj.test
services:
  web: { hostnames: [myproj.test, "*.myproj.test"], port_pool: dev }
  api: { hostnames: [api.myproj.test], port_pool: dev }
gerry init scaffolds it; gerry up (or the vite plugin) applies it; editing a hostname and restarting re-assigns it (old labels are pruned). gerry status diagnoses the stack when anything misbehaves.

docs.title: Host mode
docs.text:
Run the gerry daemon directly on the machine instead of in docker. This is the recommended end-state for local dev: supervised backends work (the proxy and your dev processes share a host, so gerry boots them on first request and sleeps them when idle), file-watching never crosses a VM boundary, and one hop of latency disappears.

gerry service install     # launchd user agent + starter config (~/.gerrymander/gerry.yaml)
gerry service status
gerry service restart
gerry service uninstall

Validated lifecycle (2026-08-14, uvicorn behind a host proxy):

step observed cold start first request held 0.87s while the process booted + health-gated, then 200 warm 4ms idle stopped after the manifest's idle_timeout re-wake 448ms on the next request, same sticky port

docs.title: Reaching the registry from inside a container
docs.text:
A host-mode daemon binds 127.0.0.1:4780, which no container can reach. Widening api.listen to 0.0.0.0 fixes that and publishes your registry to every machine on the network at the same time.

extra_listen adds listeners without touching that decision. The @docker sentinel expands to the host's docker bridge gateway addresses — the addresses containers already resolve host.docker.internal to, and the only ones they can use. Docker bridge subnets are not routed off the host, so the result stays as private as loopback:

api:
  listen: 127.0.0.1:4780
  extra_listen: ["@docker"]        # or "@docker:4781" to use another port

Then, from inside any container:

GERRY_API=http://host.docker.internal:4780

Notes:

  • Bare @docker reuses api.listen's port, so the registry answers on one number everywhere.
  • Gateways are resolved at startup. Creating a docker network afterwards does not add a listener — restart the daemon (gerry service restart).
  • Extra listeners never block startup: if docker is absent or a network was pruned, gerry logs and serves on api.listen alone.
  • A literal address in extra_listen (not the sentinel) is held to the same rule as api.listen: off-host and keyless is refused.

docs.title: Migrating a machine from the container daemon
docs.text:
The container and host daemons want the same ports (80/443/517x/4780), so this is a swap, not a coexistence:

  1. Convert docker-alias backends. Container-mode manifests reach docker-network aliases (address: my-app:80); a host daemon cannot dial those directly. Change each to the docker: backend form, docker: { network: <net>, host: my-app, port: 80 }, and gerry maintains a socat relay on that network automatically (no compose edits, no published ports). Host processes use address:/supervised: as usual.
  2. Copy the CA so browser trust survives: cp deploy/dev/data/ca/* ~/.gerrymander/ca/
  3. Copy or re-seed the registry: either move the SQLite file from the container volume to ~/.gerrymander/gerry.db, or re-run gerry up in each project (sticky ports live in the DB; copy it to keep them).
  4. Swap: docker compose down (deploy/dev) → gerry service install.
  5. gerry status should go all-green; every hostname serves as before.

Rollback is the reverse: gerry service uninstall → docker compose up -d in deploy/dev.

docs.title: Kubernetes
docs.text: In production, gerry is the authority on who owns which hostname: the missing referee between your app's tenant table and your ingress routes. It layers three capabilities; each is independently optional.

docs.title: Install
docs.text:
helm install gerry deploy/helm/gerrymander \
  --set zones[0].name=yourdomain.com \
  --set monitoring.serviceMonitor=true --set monitoring.prometheusRule=true
kubectl create secret generic gerrymander-api --from-literal=key=$(openssl rand -hex 24)

(Or the plain manifests in deploy/k8s/.) The API serves on 4780; metrics on a separate port (9091) so an ingress in front of the API can never expose them. The daemon refuses to start off-loopback with no API key.

docs.title: 1. Observer (read-only audit)
docs.text:
Polls Traefik IngressRoutes and Kubernetes Ingresses and compares them with the registry:

  • unregistered hostnames → auto-registered as platform allocations (or reported, your choice)
  • routes serving a tenant's hostname → kind-mismatch conflict
  • the same hostname served from two namespaces → duplicate-route
  • bare-Host routes that tie with a tenant catch-all's priority → shadowed-host (the classic Traefik trap where a tie silently loses traffic)

Conflicts appear at /v1/conflicts, as gerry_conflicts metrics, and as Prometheus alerts. The observer never mutates Kubernetes resources.

docs.title: Retiring disappeared hosts
docs.text:
Temporary routes (for example streaming sessions) otherwise accumulate active registry records after Kubernetes deletes them. Enable reconciliation explicitly:

observer:
  enabled: true
  zones: [yourdomain.com]
  auto_register: true
  retire_missing: true       # default false; requires auto_register
  missing_grace_period: 5m   # default 5m
  interval: 60s

Helm exposes these as observer.retireMissing and observer.missingGracePeriod. Start with retirement disabled to inspect status.observation and the missing-host metric, then back up the registry before enabling it for an existing installation. Existing records receive a fresh absence window; their age is never evidence of disappearance.

Only active source=observed, kind=platform allocations without routing backends or reservation expiry qualify. API claims, seed reservations and tenant allocations are excluded. A host must be absent from both complete, paginated lists, across at least three successful observations and the full grace period. Failed requests, malformed lists, expired/repeated pagination tokens, changed resource versions, restarts and gaps over two polling intervals reset the absence window. No retirement occurs from partial results.

Identity uses zone plus label, including wildcard labels and nested zones, so an owner replacement or another route serving the same host keeps the allocation alive. status.observation exposes last_seen_at, owner_uid, missing_since and missing_observations. Rediscovery clears absence state.

Retirement atomically writes a retire-missing event containing the complete allocation snapshot, then frees the label for a future claim or rediscovery. Kubernetes routes are never deleted by this process. The existing hold_ttl continues to apply only to pending reservations. This observer setting does not enable expiry for local development or API-managed services.

Metrics on the dedicated metrics listener:

  • gerry_observer_last_success_timestamp_seconds — last complete successful sync
  • gerry_observer_errors_total — failed cycles
  • gerry_observed_hosts_missing{zone} — absent records awaiting retirement
  • gerry_observed_hosts_retired_total{zone} — completed audited retirements

For an enabled observer, alert when the last successful sync is more than a few polling intervals old. Missing counts can rise briefly during normal session churn; sustained growth with no retirements warrants investigation.

docs.title: 2. Actuator (write-side, off by default)
docs.text:
Give an allocation a service backend and the actuator materializes a route for it:

actuator:
  enabled: true
  provider: traefik-crd     # or gateway-api
  zones: [yourdomain.com]
  entry_points: [websecure] # traefik-crd
  # gateway: { name: edge, namespace: infra }   # gateway-api

The safety contract, enforced by construction and proven by a k3d e2e in CI on every change:

  1. it lists and mutates only resources labeled app.gerrymander/managed=true
  2. hand-edited drift on a managed route is repaired within one interval
  3. releasing the allocation deletes the managed route
  4. a foreign route is never touched, ever

With traefik-crd, route priority is floored above tenant catch-alls, so the shadow trap is unrepresentable. With gateway-api, hostname precedence is by spec and wildcards use the native *. form.

docs.title: 3. GitOps input (HostnameReservation CRD)
docs.text:
apiVersion: gerrymander.dev/v1alpha1
kind: HostnameReservation
metadata: { name: grafana, namespace: infra }
spec:
  zone: yourdomain.com
  label: grafana
  kind: platform

Enable crd_ingest and CRs feed the registry. The CR is input; the database is truth. A reservation that loses the race for a taken label logs the conflict and stays unfulfilled; it never steals the name. Deleting the CR releases the allocation (only CRD-owned ones).

docs.title: Wiring your app
docs.text: Your app claims tenant hostnames at signup through the API (a Laravel client ships in clients/laravel; the API is four endpoints for any other stack). Use scoped tokens so the app's credential can only touch tenant claims. The result is a closed loop: signup → claim (reserved names enforced) → actuator creates the route → observer stays quiet because it recognizes gerry's own work → Prometheus alerts on anything that drifts.

docs.title: Any TLD you like
docs.text:
.test is a default, not a requirement. Zones are just names:

gerry zone add --name myapp.internal --profile dev
export GERRY_TLD=internal    # gerry init now scaffolds <project>.internal

gerry setup derives resolver wiring from the zones the daemon actually has, whatever their TLD. Three TLDs deserve caution:

TLD Why .dev, .app Real, Google-owned, HSTS-preloaded: browsers force HTTPS and refuse untrusted certs with no bypass. Workable only after gerry trust. .local Owned by mDNS/Bonjour; resolvers treat it specially. Avoid. .localhost Browsers hardwire it to loopback — fine locally, useless on a tailnet.

.test is IETF-reserved for exactly this purpose, which is why it is the default; .internal is the other officially blessed choice.

docs.title: Several machines running gerry
docs.text:
Each daemon is its own registry. The one rule that keeps this sane: one zone, one authority. Never register the same zone on two daemons — two registries answering for one namespace is precisely the race gerry exists to remove.

Three patterns that follow from it:

docs.title: 1. One authority, many clients
docs.text:
One machine runs the daemon; the others talk to it:

# on a second machine (no daemon needed)
export GERRY_API=http://100.x.y.z:4780   # the authority, over the tailnet
gerry ls
gerry claim --zone myapp.test --label api
GERRY_API=http://100.x.y.z:4780 gerry trust   # once, for its CA

Backends still need to be reachable from the proxy machine (tailnet IPs work as backend addresses).

docs.title: 2. A zone per machine
docs.text:
Each machine owns its own namespace and runs the full stack:

# laptop:   zones: [mac.test]
# desktop:  zones: [desk.test]

Tailnet split DNS routes are per domain, so each zone can point at its machine: mac.test → 100.x.y.1, desk.test → 100.x.y.2. Every device then resolves app.mac.test to the laptop and app.desk.test to the desktop. gerry tailnet on each machine walks through its own row.

docs.title: 3. Same project, moving between machines
docs.text: Keep the manifest in the repo (it already is: gerrymander.yaml) and let whichever machine you're on claim it in that machine's zone — or use pattern 1 so the claim lives in one registry regardless of where you type. Sticky ports are per-registry: pattern 1 gives you the same port everywhere, pattern 2 gives each machine its own.

docs.title: Quickstart
docs.text: From nothing to https://my-app.test with trusted TLS, and an understanding of what actually happened.

docs.title: 1. Install
docs.text:
curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Nano112/gerrymander/main/install.sh | sh

One command: platform detected, binary installed, then gerry bootstrap runs automatically: daemon on login, DNS for dev zones, TLS trust. With brew it's two: brew install nano112/tap/gerry && gerry bootstrap. GERRY_INSTALL_ONLY=1 skips the bootstrap if you want the pieces separately (steps 2–3 below are what it does for you).

docs.title: 2. Run the daemon
docs.text:
gerry service install    # launchd on macOS, systemd --user on Linux
gerry status             # doctor: daemon / DNS / proxy / trust checklist

The daemon is the registry (SQLite at ~/.gerrymander/gerry.db), a TLS proxy with its own local CA, an embedded DNS server for dev TLDs, and a process supervisor.

docs.title: 3. Wire the machine, reversibly
docs.text:
gerry setup

This routes dev TLDs (like .test) to gerry's DNS and installs the CA into your trust store. Every file it writes is marker-tagged; TLDs that already resolve (dnsmasq, Herd) are skipped, and gerry uninstall removes only gerry's own marks, so it can never break DNS it didn't set up. See Coexistence for the full interference matrix.

docs.title: 4. A project
docs.text:
cd my-app
gerry init               # writes gerrymander.yaml

# gerrymander.yaml
project: my-app
zone: my-app.test
services:
  frontend:
    hostnames: [my-app.test]
    dev: "bun run dev"
  api:
    hostnames: [api.my-app.test]
    dev: "uv run uvicorn main:app --port {PORT} --reload"

Then either:

gerry dev                # run everything: ports granted, manifest applied,
                         # prefixed output, group shutdown

or, for Vite projects, add the plugin and forget gerry exists:

// vite.config.js
import gerrymander from "gerrymander-vite";
export default { plugins: [gerrymander()] };

bun run dev now applies the manifest, gets the service's sticky port, and serves https://my-app.test with working HMR over TLS.

docs.title: 5. Containers too
docs.text:
# docker-compose.yml
services:
  api:
    image: my-api
    labels:
      - gerrymander.hostname=api.my-app.test
      # optional: gerrymander.port=8080, gerrymander.network=mynet

docker compose up claims the hostname and routes to the container (even with no published ports; gerry maintains a relay). down releases it.

docs.title: What just happened
docs.text:
• my-app.test and api.my-app.test are allocations in a local registry. gerry ls shows them, gerry rename api.my-app.test api2 renames atomically, releasing frees the name.
  • Ports are sticky per owner: the same service gets the same port tomorrow, from a pool that avoids 3000/5173/8000/8080.
  • The proxy's 404/502 pages are diagnostic and self-recovering: they tell you which backend is down and reload when it returns.

The same registry, with the same semantics, runs in production. See Kubernetes.

docs.title: The desktop app
docs.text: The Map view traces every hostname to its backend; Districts manages claims; Ports shows every listener cross-marked with registry grants.

docs.title: nginx and Nginx Proxy Manager
docs.text:
gerry's embedded proxy is one dataplane, not the only one. If a machine already runs nginx (or Nginx Proxy Manager), the registry can drive it: allocations stay the source of truth, your proxy keeps serving.

Both writers follow the safety contract used everywhere else in gerry: they mark what they create and only ever touch marked things.

docs.title: Plain nginx: nginx_sync
docs.text:
Renders active allocations with address backends into one include file and reloads:

nginx_sync:
  enabled: true
  conf_path: /opt/homebrew/etc/nginx/servers/gerry.conf
  listen: "80"                # or "443 ssl" with your own cert directives
  reload_cmd: nginx -s reload # "" = write only

The file starts with a marker line; a pre-existing file without the marker is refused, never overwritten. Server blocks carry websocket upgrade headers and X-Forwarded-*; the @local backend sentinel becomes 127.0.0.1. Everything outside that one file (your nginx.conf, other server blocks, certificates) is invisible to gerry.

docs.title: Nginx Proxy Manager: npm_sync
docs.text:
NPM keeps its nginx internal, so this writer speaks NPM's REST API instead: allocations become proxy hosts, visible and editable in the NPM UI alongside everything you made by hand.

npm_sync:
  enabled: true
  url: http://100.71.144.24:81       # the NPM admin API
  # identity_env: NPM_IDENTITY        (defaults shown)
  # secret_env:   NPM_SECRET
  local_host: host.docker.internal    # what "@local" forwards to
  zones: [myzone.test]

Each created proxy host carries # gerrymander-managed in its advanced config; hosts made in the UI never match and are never touched. Releasing an allocation deletes its proxy host; hand-edited drift on a managed host is repaired on the next pass. Certificates and access lists remain NPM's job — attach them in the UI as usual (gerry does not overwrite fields it does not manage on update... it manages domain names, forwarding target and the marker).

Pair either writer with Tailscale DNS advertising and a zone resolves tailnet-wide while nginx on one machine serves it.

docs.title: Tailscale
docs.text: Your dev hostnames can resolve from every machine on your tailnet: the laptop, the work machine, your phone. One config line makes gerry's DNS answer with this machine's tailnet address instead of loopback; split DNS on the tailnet routes the dev TLD here.

docs.title: The guided way
docs.text:
gerry tailnet

probes the three routes below against your actual tailnet — which already work, which don't — and prints the exact steps for whatever is missing. Re-running it verifies each change as you make it. The rest of this page is the same material in prose.

docs.title: On the machine running gerry
docs.text:
dns:
  enabled: true
  listen: ":53"          # must be reachable from peers, not loopback
  zones: [test]
  advertise: tailscale   # answers carry this machine's tailnet IPv4

advertise also accepts a literal IP. With an IPv4 advertised, AAAA queries return empty on purpose: handing a peer ::1 for a remote machine would break resolution.

The proxy already listens on all interfaces (proxy.tls: ":443"), so peers reach it as soon as they can resolve it.

docs.title: On the tailnet (split DNS)
docs.text:
Point the dev TLD at this machine's tailnet IP.

Tailscale admin console: DNS → Split DNS → domain test, nameserver 100.x.y.z (this machine).

Headscale: in the config's dns section:

dns:
  split:
    test: ["100.x.y.z"]

docs.title: Trust on the peers
docs.text:
TLS still comes from gerry's local CA, so each peer that should get a green padlock needs it once:

GERRY_API=http://100.x.y.z:4780 gerry trust

(/v1/ca is unauthenticated by design; the CA certificate is public material.) Phones: open http://100.x.y.z:4780/v1/ca.crt in the browser — it downloads as a named certificate the OS knows how to install — or skip trust and accept the warning.

docs.title: No console access? The machine-name route
docs.text:
True subdomains of a MagicDNS name (app.macbook.….ts.net) cannot resolve — MagicDNS has no wildcards. The closest thing that works, with a real browser-trusted certificate and zero admin-console changes:

tailscale serve --bg --https=8443 http://127.0.0.1:<sticky-port>

gives https://<machine>.<tailnet>.ts.net:8443 tailnet-wide. Ports 443, 8443 and 10000 are available, so this scales to three apps; beyond that, split DNS is the answer. The gerrymander-vite plugin allows the machine's MagicDNS name automatically, so vite accepts these proxied requests.

gerry status detects both tailnet traps: a TLS-terminating serve handler on :443 in front of the proxy (custom SNI dies before gerry sees it), and an advertised zone with no split-DNS route (peers can't resolve, phones show "site can't be reached"). Each warning carries its exact fix.

docs.title: What this is good for
docs.text:
• Opening https://myapp.test from a phone on the tailnet to test mobile layouts against your dev server.
  • A second dev machine using the first one's hostnames and registry (GERRY_API=http://100.x.y.z:4780 gerry ls).
  • Demoing to a colleague on the tailnet without deploying anything.

Port 53 needs root or a capability on most systems; gerry service install runs the daemon as your user, so either grant the binary CAP_NET_BIND_SERVICE (Linux), keep DNS on a high port with a forwarder in front, or run split DNS against a per-zone high-port setup if your tailnet DNS supports it (Tailscale's does not; headscale forwards to :53).

docs.title: Scoped tokens
docs.text:
The root API key can do everything. That's fine for you; it's wrong for the tenant self-service portal, the CI job, or the neighboring team's service. Scoped tokens are the separation:

gerry token create tenant-acme --owner-ref acme-uuid --zone yourdomain.com
# token tenant-acme (owner, owner acme-uuid, zones yourdomain.com)
#
#   gk_9f2c…                       ← shown exactly once

docs.title: What an owner-scoped token can do
docs.text:
Operation Behavior claim forced to the token's owner_ref, kind tenant, allowed zones only list sees only its own allocations get / rename / renew / release own allocations only, 403 otherwise patch spec only, never state or labels audit GET /v1/allocations/{id}/events for its own allocations everything else 403: zones, ports, manifest apply, processes, conflicts, token management

Every rule above is pinned by a test (internal/api/scopes_test.go). The scope model is part of the public contract, not an implementation detail.

docs.title: Mechanics
docs.text:
• Plaintext is gk_ + 48 hex chars, shown once at creation. Only the SHA-256 is stored.
  • gerry token revoke <name> disables it immediately and permanently; mint a new one to restore access.
  • gerry token ls shows scope, owner, zones, last use, and revocation state (metadata only, never secrets).
  • The root API key keeps working unchanged; keyless loopback dev mode is unaffected.

docs.title: Audit trail
docs.text:
Every allocation carries an append-only event history: claimed, renamed, renewed, released, by whom, from what state.

curl -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" \
  https://gerry.yourdomain.com/v1/allocations/42/events

Owner tokens see their own allocations' history; admins see everything.

docs.title: Catalog readers
docs.text: gerry token create infra-catalog --scope catalog-read grants read-only access to the entire catalog and its logo assets. It cannot read allocations or ports, publish metadata, change routes or manage tokens. Owner tokens cannot read the catalog. This scope is registry-wide: zone and owner restrictions are not supported. Keep the token server-side. See the catalog contract.
